intrinsic_value_estimate: About $81 per share in the conservative case. Range: about $49 (pessimistic) to about $152 (if the record continues). Method: owner earnings (brk-letter-1986) of about $2.60 per share, range $2.25–$2.85. That is 1988 net income available to common of $1,038M, plus D&A of $170M, minus an assumed $250M of maintenance capex, over 364.6M average shares. Valued in two stages. Conservative case: 10% growth for 10 years, then 5%, discounted at 10%. Record case: 15%, then 5%, at 9%. Pessimistic case: $2.25 base, 7%, then 4%, at 10%. The affiliates are worth about $2.2B at market (carrying value $1.91B plus $291M excess), which adds roughly $3–4 per share not fully counted above. The net-working-capital test (bpl-letter-1965) gives about $0.22 per share. It is set aside because the 1987–89 writings (brk-letter-1987#18, brk-letter-1981#3) replace bargain hunting with buying outstanding businesses at sensible prices.
margin_of_safety: At $46.56 (close on 1989-02-24): about 42% below the conservative $81 value, about 69% below the record-case $152, and about 5% below the pessimistic $49. The framework sets no numerical hurdle. The test in force is whether the price makes sense even if the future only resembles the past (brk-letter-1981#3), and it passes: the price implies owner-earnings growth of only about 3–4% a year forever, against 12–16% compounding in 1983–88.

key_reasons.reason: The core business earns very high returns on equity and on total capital without needing leverage. The headline 33% ROE is partly due to buybacks and debt, but the unlevered core return is even higher.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §3 Business analysis: return on equity, not EPS growth, is the primary test (brk-letter-1979)
key_reasons.evidence: 1988 return on average common equity 33.3% (1988 AR). ROE was 21–23% in 1978–81, when debt was only 4–9% of capital. 1988 soft-drink pretax operating income of $1,691M on $3,809M of identifiable assets is about 44% (about 29% after tax). From 1985 to 1988, soft-drink assets rose about $754M while operating income rose about $861M.

key_reasons.reason: A wide moat that is getting wider, built on the trademark and the global distribution system. Pricing power shows up in rising margins through tax cuts and higher advertising.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §3 Durable competitive advantage, the moat (brk-letter-1986#16). Franchise strength shown by keeping the benefit of tax cuts (brk-letter-1986#22)
key_reasons.evidence: World share of flavored carbonated soft drinks rose from under 38% (1980) to nearly 45% (1988), more than double the next competitor. U.S. share is over 40%. 1986 U.S. fountain share 59%. Landor's 1988 surveys put the brand 'off the charts'. Gross margin (restated basis) rose from 50.5% (1985) to 55.6% (1988) while the statutory tax rate fell from 46% to 34% and advertising rose from $648M to $842M. International consumption is about 51 servings per person against 274 in the U.S.

key_reasons.reason: Earnings turn into cash. Owner earnings are close to reported earnings, and growth needs little capital.
key_reasons.evidence: 1988 operating cash flow $1,167M against net income $1,045M. Capex $387M against D&A $170M. Owner earnings estimated at about $2.60 per share (range $2.25–$2.85). Management calls soft drinks 'a low capital requirement' business.

key_reasons.reason: Retained earnings have produced several dollars of market value for each dollar kept.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §4 Each $1 retained must create at least $1 of market value (brk-letter-1983)
key_reasons.evidence: 1984–88: about $1.89B retained (reinvested earnings went from $2,494M to $4,385M). Market value rose from about $7.3B to about $15.8B after about $2.2B of buybacks, roughly $4.50 per $1 retained. Per share: $4.96 retained against a $26.80 price gain. Holding the P/E constant, the ratio is still about 3.9x.

key_reasons.reason: Management bought back large amounts of stock at moderate multiples, slowed when the price was high, and reversed its move outside the core business. This shows a shareholder orientation, not empire-building.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §4 Buybacks only well below intrinsic value (brk-letter-1984#4). Honest, able management in place (brk-letter-1979)
key_reasons.evidence: 69.4M shares repurchased 1984–88 at an average of about $31.55: 11.6x earnings in 1984, about 14x in 1988, only 2.9M shares in 1986 at about 18.5x. Shares outstanding fell from about 409M to 354.8M. Entertainment was spun into a 49%-owned affiliate (1987), with plastics, South Africa and coffee also exited. The same team has run the company since 1981 under an explicit 12% cost-of-capital hurdle.

key_reasons.reason: The price makes sense even if the future is considerably worse than the past.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §5 Valuation, as applied in force by 1989: an outstanding business at a sensible price, priced to make sense if the future resembles the past (brk-letter-1987#18, brk-letter-1981#3)
key_reasons.evidence: $46.56 is 16.3x 1988 EPS of $2.85 and about 17.9x owner earnings of $2.60. EPS compounded at 11.6% (1978–88) and 16.1% (1983–88). 1989 guidance is for EPS growth 'well into the mid-teens' (upi-1989-01-31). The price implies only about 3–4% perpetual growth at a 9–10% discount rate.

key_reasons.reason: No catalyst is needed and there is no reason to wait. The market will reflect business results over time.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §6 No catalyst needed; Mr. Market is there to serve, not to guide (brk-letter-1987)
key_reasons.evidence: The stock fell from $53.13 to $28.96 in October 1987, traded at $35–40 through much of 1988, and is now $46.56, while business value compounded the whole time. 16.3x trailing earnings is below the 1987 peak of about 22x.

key_reasons.reason: The facts are clear and the risk to underlying value is low, which justifies a concentrated position, sized below the maximum for the remaining uncertainties.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §7 Concentrate when the facts are clear, up to 40% (bpl-letter-1965)
key_reasons.evidence: Ten-year documented record, simple concentrate business (over 90% of operating income), and a conservative-case margin of safety of about 42%. Kept below 40% because of currency exposure (76% of operating income abroad), a net debt-to-capital ratio of 24.3%, and Berkshire's capital not being in the packet.

risks: Currency: about 76% of operating income is earned abroad. The dollar's decline (key currencies up 27%, 16% and 10% in 1986–88) inflated recent growth, and a stronger dollar would reverse that.

Leverage by choice: total debt is 38.8% of capital and management targets a net 35% ceiling to lower its cost of capital. There are also about $133M of bottler debt guarantees and $101M of the entertainment affiliate's receivables under guarantee.
Low-return affiliates: the U.S. bottling affiliate earned about 8% on its equity in 1988, and the entertainment affiliate ($598M carrying value) is hit-driven and has had repeated write-downs.
Foods has no moat: frozen and chilled orange juice volumes fell 22% and 6% in 1988, and returns are near the cost of capital.
Trademark mishandling: the 1985 reformulation shows the brand can be damaged by management decisions.
Most U.S. bottler contracts set Brand A syrup prices by formula, which limits domestic pricing freedom. Latin American inflation also compresses margins.
Compensation is tied to stock price with no return hurdle, and option grants rose to 4.18M in 1988. Insider ownership is not in the packet.
The buyback rule is framed around excess cash rather than price against value, so the company could keep buying at full prices.
Owner earnings depend on an assumed maintenance-capex figure. The packet gives no maintenance/growth split and no long-term Treasury yield for the discount rate.
Accumulating a large stake will push up the purchase price.
what_would_change_my_mind: Constant-currency results showing that the underlying growth in international operating income is far below what was reported.
Evidence that maintenance capex is far above $250M a year, which would push owner earnings toward $2.25 or below.
A long-term Treasury yield well above 11–12% on the as-of date, which would compress the conservative value toward $60.
A proxy statement showing negligible stock ownership by management or directors, or self-serving compensation.
Talking with management and finding that buybacks are not tied to any view of intrinsic value, or that large new diversification outside beverages is planned.
A falling world share or shrinking gross margins, which would indicate the moat is eroding.
The price running far ahead of value (for example, well above $80–100 before the position is built), which would mean pausing purchases rather than reversing.
sell_triggers: A lasting loss of the franchise: sustained loss of world or U.S. share, or an inability to raise prices, shown by gross margin falling for several years.

Management turning against shareholders: large share issuance for low-value acquisitions (the brk-letter-1982#17 standard), or an expensive return to businesses outside beverages like the 1982 studio purchase.
Balance-sheet leverage rising well beyond the 35% net debt-to-capital ceiling to fund non-core uses.
Evidence of misleading reporting, which would break the candor test of brk-letter-1983#2.
Not a trigger: a higher price on its own. The default under §8 is a permanent holding (brk-letter-1987#18).
